title: The Spirit of the Lord Is on Me: Good News to the Poor
summary: An anointed speaker announces that the Spirit of the Lord GOD is on him to bring good news to the poor, bind up the brokenhearted, proclaim liberty to captives, and announce the year of the LORD's favor. Mourners in Zion will receive beauty for ashes and will become oaks of righteousness who rebuild ancient ruins, while the nations serve them and they are called priests of the LORD in an everlasting covenant. The chapter ends with a song of joy from one clothed in garments of salvation like a bridegroom or bride.
story: This chapter stands at the center of the bright vision of chapters 60 to 62. Chapter 60 described Zion's glory; chapter 61 introduces the one who brings it about, an anointed messenger. His words recall the Servant, on whom God put his Spirit (42:1), and the herald of good news (40:9; 52:7), and they echo the promises of release to prisoners (42:7; 49:9). They also answer the promise at the end of chapter 59 that God's Spirit and words would rest on his people. What was promised to Zion in chapter 60 is here announced as a mission.
historical:
The chapter's setting, like that of chapters 56 to 66 as a whole, is most often placed among the community in Judah after the return from Babylon, a people of ruins, poverty, and mourning (verses 3 and 4 speak of devastations of many generations). On the traditional view, the eighth-century prophet speaks ahead to that community. Who the speaker is has been debated. Some read him as the prophet himself describing his own calling; others as the Servant of the earlier songs, since he is Spirit-endowed and sent to the afflicted, and some scholars even call this passage a fifth Servant Song; others as a royal or messianic figure, since anointing was given to kings. These views are not mutually exclusive.

The chapter was important in Judaism before the New Testament. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, a text known as 11QMelchizedek combines Isaiah 61 with the jubilee law of Leviticus 25 and describes a heavenly figure, Melchizedek, who will proclaim liberty and bring about the day of God's favor and judgment. This shows that Jews around the first century were already reading Isaiah 61 as a description of a future deliverer.
cultural:
Anointing with oil set people apart for a task: priests (Exodus 29:7), kings (1 Samuel 16:13), and occasionally prophets (1 Kings 19:16). The one anointed was said to have the Spirit of the LORD come upon him, as with David. Here the anointing is the Spirit himself.

The proclamation of liberty draws on the jubilee law of Leviticus 25. Every fiftieth year, debts were to be released, Israelite slaves set free, and family land returned to its original owners; the word “liberty” (deror) in verse 1 is the same word used in Leviticus 25:10. Whether the jubilee was ever fully practiced is uncertain, but the ideal was well known. The exchanges of verse 3 draw on customs of mourning and celebration: mourners put ashes on their heads, while a festive headdress and anointing oil marked joy. In Hebrew, “beauty” (peer) and “ashes” (epher) sound alike, a play the English cannot show. In verse 10 the bridegroom's headdress is described with a verb used of priests, and a bride's jewels completed her wedding attire.
literary: The chapter has three parts. In verses 1 to 3 the anointed speaker describes his commission in a rush of infinitives: to preach, to bind up, to proclaim, to comfort, to console, to give. Verses 4 to 9 describe the results for Zion's people, with God himself speaking in verses 8 and 9: they rebuild ruins, receive a double portion, and enter an everlasting covenant. Verses 10 and 11 are a song of response, sung by a voice that may be Zion herself, the prophet, or the anointed one, clothed in salvation and righteousness. The chapter moves from mourning to rejoicing, and its last image, a garden making seeds spring up, echoes the oaks of righteousness in verse 3.

outline.t: The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me: the anointed one's mission
Ruins rebuilt, priests of the LORD, a double portion
God loves justice: an everlasting covenant
Clothed with salvation like a bride and bridegroom

doctrines.note: “The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me” (verse 1). The Spirit anoints for mission, and the mission is to the poor, the brokenhearted, captives, and mourners. In the Old Testament the Spirit equips particular people for God's work.
Anointed translates the Hebrew verb from which Messiah (anointed one) comes. The chapter describes a Spirit-anointed figure who brings liberation, and Jesus claims this role in Luke 4.
Salvation here is concrete: release, healing of broken hearts, comfort, rebuilding, and joy. The righteous garments of verse 10 are given, not earned; the speaker says God has clothed him.
“You will be called the priests of the LORD” (verse 6). The whole people become a priesthood, fulfilling the calling of Exodus 19:6, a theme the New Testament applies to the church (1 Peter 2:9).

words.note: Mashach, to anoint, to pour or smear oil on someone to set them apart. The noun mashiach, anointed one, becomes the title Messiah, and its Greek translation, Christos, gives us Christ. Kings, priests, and occasionally prophets were anointed; here the LORD has anointed the speaker, and the anointing is the gift of his Spirit.

Deror, liberty, release. It is the technical word for the release proclaimed in the year of jubilee (Leviticus 25:10) and in Jeremiah 34 when Jerusalem briefly freed its slaves. Using it here frames the anointed one's announcement as a jubilee: debts canceled, captives freed, inheritance restored.

Ratson, favor, acceptance, goodwill. “The year of the LORD’s favor” (verse 2) is the time when God shows his goodwill and acceptance. It stands in contrast with “the day of our God’s vengeance” in the same verse: a year of favor, a day of vengeance.

christ: Luke 4:16-21 is one of the most important scenes in the Gospels. In the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus is handed the scroll of Isaiah, reads verses 1 and 2, rolls up the scroll, sits down, and says that this Scripture has been fulfilled in their hearing. He stops before the words about the day of our God's vengeance, and many interpreters see in that pause the difference between his first coming, the year of favor, and a final judgment still to come. Luke's wording follows the Greek Old Testament, which includes recovery of sight for the blind, and adds a line from 58:6 about setting the oppressed free. When John the Baptist later asks whether Jesus is the one to come, Jesus answers by pointing to the blind seeing and the poor hearing good news (Matthew 11:4-5; Luke 7:22), echoing this chapter. The Beatitudes' blessing on those who mourn, that they will be comforted (Matthew 5:4), carries the same note. This is one of the clearest cases where Jesus identifies himself with an Isaiah passage.

hard.q: Why did Jesus stop reading in the middle of a sentence in Luke 4?
hard.a: Verse 2 speaks of both “the year of the LORD’s favor” and “the day of our God’s vengeance,” but in Luke 4:19 Jesus stops after the first phrase. Readers have long noticed this. One common explanation is that Jesus was marking the character of his present ministry as a time of grace, with judgment reserved for a later day, a pattern that runs through the New Testament's teaching about his two comings. Others caution against building too much on the omission, since synagogue readings could be short and Luke does not comment on it; some suggest the ending simply fit what Jesus wanted to announce that day. Either way, the rest of Luke's Gospel does not deny judgment (Luke 21:22 speaks of days of vengeance), but it places the emphasis of Jesus's arrival on favor and release.

questions: Jesus chose this passage to describe his own mission. What does it tell you about what he cares about?
Verse 3 promises beauty for ashes and praise for despair. Where do you need that exchange, and how do you wait for it honestly?
Those who are comforted become oaks of righteousness who rebuild ruins. How has comfort you received turned into strength for others?
